overview: The Zunbils, also called Rutbils, ruled Zabulistan in southern Afghanistan, separate from but connected to Kabul’s rulers. Independence emerged after about 680. Earlier accounts describe a shrine to Zun alongside Buddhist institutions. This map’s 700 to 800 interval is only an eighth-century snapshot. Its outline includes Kandahar and part of Zamindawar but omits Ghazni, an important royal center, and Bost, sometimes within the realm. Kabul lies outside it. The boundary is therefore an incomplete approximation, not a surveyed frontier.

periods.title: The mapped eighth-century kingdom
periods.summary: Rulers exchanged embassies, resisted incursions and issued coins; royal names and exact borders remain uncertain.

sections.title: A frontier court with distant connections

items.text: Zabul’s rulers sought recognition far beyond Afghanistan. Tang records describe investitures in 720 and 738, and an embassy to China in 753. These diplomatic ties existed alongside recurring warfare and tribute demands on the western frontier.

In the 720s, the Korean pilgrim Hyecho described Zabul’s king as the Kabul king’s nephew, ruling independently. He distinguished Turkic rulers and soldiers from other inhabitants. His account reveals a politically connected but culturally diverse country, rather than one uniform ethnic kingdom.

Royal silver coins combined several languages; copper issues commonly used Middle Persian. Their designs borrowed from Sasanian and Arab-Sasanian money. A coin could carry an Iranian-looking royal portrait and several written traditions together. Its date is not always convertible securely into our calendar.

Hyecho compared Zabul’s products and clothing with neighboring Kapisi, where he listed grapes, barley, wheat, pack animals and fine-wool garments. Men and women there wore shirts, trousers and boots. This regional comparison offers useful clues to daily life, although it is not an excavated Zabul household inventory.

The same traveler reported brothers sharing a wife in Zabul and several neighboring countries, associating this arrangement with preserving a household’s livelihood. This is his broad description of family organization, not proof that every local family followed one marriage pattern.

Hyecho found Buddhist monasteries and described the chief Satakgan giving gold and silver in quantities reportedly exceeding the king’s gifts. Religious generosity could make a powerful public statement. A chief might outshine his ruler without needing a bigger crown.

sections.title: A sanctuary that needed skilled hands

items.text: Tapa Sardar near Ghazni was much older than the mapped kingdom. After a seventh-century fire, builders reconstructed its chapels around the late seventh or early eighth century. Its ruins preserve a major religious center, although the imported polygon leaves the Ghazni area outside its edge.

In Chapel 63, artists made a reclining Buddha about 15 meters long, representing his final passing into nirvana. Clay, paint and gilding produced an enormous religious image. This was sculpture on a scale that made even a grown-up visitor look very small.

How did sculptors keep everything together? At Tapa Sardar, they built yellow-clay cores mixed with straw, added red-clay surfaces, and used wooden sticks to attach heads and limbs or fasten images to walls. Seventh- and eighth-century masterpieces depended on practical knowledge of humble materials.

Fire sometimes baked these clay decorations into harder terracotta, helping fragments survive while destroying their painted finish. A dark fragment today can therefore conceal a much brighter original appearance. Damage and preservation can be parts of the same object’s story.

A surviving head of Durga from Chapel 23 is approximately 64 centimeters high. Finding this goddess within a Buddhist sanctuary is a reminder that its religious imagery drew on interconnected traditions. The head belongs to the site’s later sculptural production, broadly the seventh or eighth century.

A late-period pottery fragment from Tapa Sardar’s second terrace shows two running goats pressed into its red-clay surface. The vessel was wheel-turned and stamped. At only 9.1 centimeters across, the surviving piece preserves both a potter’s technique and a tiny animal scene.

Molded decoration on Tapa Sardar’s late-period thrones and small stupas imitated jewelry and uncut gemstones. Giulia Forgione interprets some unusual gem shapes as symbols of purity. These were clay representations of precious things, demonstrating how artists could communicate wealth and religious ideas without covering every surface in actual jewels.

On a Zabulistan coin, Harmatta and Litvinsky transcribe the short Brahmi-script legend as “šrī vākhudevah” and translate it “His Highness the Majestic Lord.” This is their scholarly Roman-letter transcription of an eighth-century royal formula, not a reproduction of the original letter shapes. Their exact ruler identification and calendar conversion are less secure than this broad attribution; the sample should not stand for everybody’s everyday speech.

Italian archaeologists investigated Tapa Sardar in the 1960s and 1970s and resumed work in 2003. Fragile clay required strengthening during excavation and careful laboratory treatment. Measurements, photographs and find locations let researchers reconstruct relationships among pieces even when the original sculptures are badly broken.

sections.title: Later conquests and an uncertain archaeological ending

items.text: After the map’s cutoff, Yaqub ibn Layth’s Saffarid armies transformed the region. A Zunbil was killed around 864 to 865, but his son Firuz recovered territory before renewed campaigns. Accounts place further fighting in the late 860s and early 870s. This was a sequence of defeats and recoveries, not an instantaneous disappearance.

Tapa Sardar’s final abandonment is a separate question. Scholars debate whether a recorded temple destruction in 795 refers to this site, while its art also has connections pointing toward the ninth century. Neither the map ending in 800 nor a convenient conquest date settles when its last worshippers left.

ending.text: Saffarid campaigns in the later ninth century broke Zunbil power in stages; sources describe Firuz’s capture in 873 after earlier recovery. The atlas stops in 800, well before these events. The political defeat concerns a ruling house, not the disappearance of southern Afghanistan’s inhabitants.
